title: BFS / DFS
summary: Breadth for distance layers; depth for exhaustive paths and components.

parts.rule: Depth-first search pushes down one branch before returning; breadth-first search expands nodes level by level from a queue. On an unweighted graph, BFS distances equal the fewest hops. DFS is the usual engine for component labeling, cycle checks, DAG ordering ideas, and backtracking. Mark nodes when first seen so cyclic edges cannot restart forever.
parts.why: Choosing the wrong walk is a frequent miss: DFS when the prompt wants fewest hops, or BFS when you must enumerate paths. Skipping the visited set loops on cycles. Saying "queue for breadth, stack or recursion for depth" shows the choice was intentional rather than accidental.
parts.example: Undirected edges link 1-2, 1-3, and 2-4. BFS from 1 starts with queue [1], then [2, 3], then [3, 4], then [4]. Distances: 1 is 0, 2 and 3 are 1, 4 is 2 — so fewest hops from 1 to 4 equal 2. A recursive DFS from 1 might visit 1 then 2 then 4, return, then visit 3, producing order 1,2,4,3. On a course DAG with edges A→B, A→C, B→D, C→D, finishing times from DFS can order a valid sequence such as A, B, C, D. Always mark a node on discovery so a back edge into 2 cannot spin forever.
parts.use: Pick BFS for hop-distance, tree level order, and bipartite coloring by layers. Pick DFS for components, cycle detection, topological ordering on DAGs, and as the skeleton under backtracking search. Say which one you chose before coding the loop.
parts.refuse: Do not use DFS when the metric is unweighted shortest path — BFS belongs there (Dijkstra once weights appear). Do not omit visited marks on graphs that may contain cycles. Do not run BFS off a stack. Do not claim a topological order while a cycle remains in the graph.

body:
Rule. Depth-first search pushes down one branch before returning; breadth-first search expands nodes level by level from a queue. On an unweighted graph, BFS distances equal the fewest hops. DFS is the usual engine for component labeling, cycle checks, DAG ordering ideas, and backtracking. Mark nodes when first seen so cyclic edges cannot restart forever.

Why it matters. Choosing the wrong walk is a frequent miss: DFS when the prompt wants fewest hops, or BFS when you must enumerate paths. Skipping the visited set loops on cycles. Saying "queue for breadth, stack or recursion for depth" shows the choice was intentional rather than accidental.

Worked example. Undirected edges link 1-2, 1-3, and 2-4. BFS from 1 starts with queue [1], then [2, 3], then [3, 4], then [4]. Distances: 1 is 0, 2 and 3 are 1, 4 is 2 — so fewest hops from 1 to 4 equal 2. A recursive DFS from 1 might visit 1 then 2 then 4, return, then visit 3, producing order 1,2,4,3. On a course DAG with edges A→B, A→C, B→D, C→D, finishing times from DFS can order a valid sequence such as A, B, C, D. Always mark a node on discovery so a back edge into 2 cannot spin forever.

When to use. Pick BFS for hop-distance, tree level order, and bipartite coloring by layers. Pick DFS for components, cycle detection, topological ordering on DAGs, and as the skeleton under backtracking search. Say which one you chose before coding the loop.

When to refuse. Do not use DFS when the metric is unweighted shortest path — BFS belongs there (Dijkstra once weights appear). Do not omit visited marks on graphs that may contain cycles. Do not run BFS off a stack. Do not claim a topological order while a cycle remains in the graph.
